utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As parties know, we have unfortunately a late start today because the courtroom was not available at our normal time. Are you ready with the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour. I believe he's available now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well then, if he could be called. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you would be kind enough to read aloud the affirmation on the card which is now offered to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you would be seated. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: My name is Sylejman Selimi. I am a major general in the protection corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you tell us your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I was born on the 25th of September, 1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I was born in the village Acareva in the Srbica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you have met with investigators for the Office of the Prosecutor before coming here to testify. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, it is right. It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you were issued a Prosecutor's summons requiring you to attend those meetings?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, it is true. I've had a summons to come here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But I'm speaking about the meetings you had earlier with investigators. You were summonsed to those meetings. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in those meetings with the Office of the Prosecutor, were you entirely truthful to the best of your ability?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I've tried to say the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you've also met previously with representatives of the Defence. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, I've met them. I had contacts with the representatives of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And as you said, you were served a subpoena issued by this Honourable Trial Chamber ordering you to appear and testify here today. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to first ask you a few questions about your personal background. Are you married?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I do apologise for interjecting. I thought it appropriate at this juncture to raise that this is the first time that we or the Defence have heard that a witness summons has been issued. We're not aware of any application to this Court for a witness summons, nor have we seen any decision from this Court for a witness summons. So it is somewhat surprising if that is the case that it hasn't been served on the Defence prior to the witness giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I could simply comment that in the practice of the Tribunal, witness summonses are usually ex parte and are dealt with confidentially to the party seeking them. That has been the practice followed in this case, as far as I am aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm glad to have that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. They may be sought on notice, but that is almost unknown in my experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I am aware of various cases before this Tribunal in which witness summonses have been requested on notice. There were several, for example, in the Celibici case. There are others that come to mind. Of course it doesn't appear to have been a matter of huge confidentiality, as particularly there had been previous contact between the Defence and the witness and indeed the Defence and the Prosecution, and the witness said he wanted to be a Defence witness. We had been very candid with the Prosecution. So it somewhat surprising that without notice option had recourse to, when it doesn't appear to have been strictly necessary. Your Honour, that's the only comment I wish to make at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: General, I was asking if you are married.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm married. But I just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a question if I'm allowed to ask a question here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you're wanting to put a question to the Chamber, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'd like to put a question to the Chamber if I'm allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you know, I've been invited with a summons as it was explained here, however I'm here in the quality of a witness. Am I here in the quality as an eyewitness, as it has been spoken, which -- to talk about the prison camp of Lapusnik? Or I'm a witness in the process of Lapusnik, or I'm here as a witness in the trial of the UCK? This is my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're here as a witness. You will be asked questions about matters which either the prosecuting or the defence counsel think are relevant to their -- to this case. You are not categorised in the categories that you posed in your question. You are simply a witness, and it is expected that you will seek to answer any question put to you either by prosecuting or defence counsel as accurately as you can, and truthfully.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, General, just please try to answer my questions to the best of your ability, to the best of your memory, to the best of your knowledge. I understand that you're married and that you have children. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm married and I have one daughter and one son.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Would you tell the Chamber, please, about your educational background, how far you went in school, whether you had any higher education after high school.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: After finishing the high school in [inaudible] in Klina, then I graduated from the metallurgical faculty in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And after high school did you perform any military service?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: After completing my military service -- sorry, after completing my high school, I joined the military service of former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what year was that? How long were you in the service at that period?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: The service, the military service was obligatory, and it was one year service. After finishing -- right after finishing the high school, then I joined the military service of former Yugoslavia in Montenegro, mainly in Trovrh or Tivar [phoen] as it is known in Albanian, and I completed it in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've told us the town you were born in. Have you spent most of your life in that town, in that area?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, I've spent most of my life there and I live there as well now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At any point did you spend any time living abroad?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: No, I've not lived abroad, but I've travelled quite often abroad because my father worked in Germany and I visited many other countries such as Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you just -- and we'll move own soon, but tell me what period you were in Germany and what you did while you were in Germany.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Very often I have joined my father, to visit my father there because he was a worker there in Germany. And for some time I played with a club there because I'm a sportsman, and I played with a club Vidan Pes [phoen]. It is with the third league in Germany. This has been a very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when did you return from Germany to your village?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I returned in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I just went there temporarily. I didn't go there to stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'd like to briefly go over your military career from your first involvement up until your present position as major general. Let's start with January in 1997. Did you join any military or any military organisation at that time?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, I joined the military organisation -- even before 1997 I was in the military group of Adem Jashari. As you know, the war was unavoidable and I would not like to repeat the events that occurred up to the period, eviction of people from work. And I also joined the group of Adem Jashari just right after the event of Prekaz and even later. While in 1997, as you said, I've been a member and even before 1997 of the Kosovo Liberation Army since its foundation. However, the rank and the duty that you have mentioned earlier, I've taken here as a commander of the Drenica operational zone, the first operational zone of Drenica. And this was in May 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And what was the next post or command you had after being commander of the Drenica zone, being appointed to that post in May 1998?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: After that in 1999, let's say February 1999 -- it is the period of the Rambouillet delegation -- I was elected commander of the General Staff, the UCK general headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And following on, can you just tell us whatever other posts, commands, you may have held.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: At the same time with the interim government -- with the formation of the interim government of Kosovo, I was appointed a commander of the Kosova Protection Corps, as well as I was appointed commander of the guard that was supposed to found this corps. For the time being, I'm a deputy commander of the Kosova Protection Corps and I have the post of major general.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And to be just a little bit more specific, can you tell the Chamber what period you were commander of the General Staff of the KLA, from when to when.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I have taken this position as a commander of the General Staff of the KLA from February 1999, from 18th to 20th February, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you started talking about how even before 1997 you were involved with what would become the Kosovo Liberation Army and that war was inevitable. Can you tell us, please, when you first -- in your opinion, when you first became involved in this effort, in this cause?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I became involved in this effort since the foundation of the KLA, and I consider myself a member since the KLA was founded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when do you consider that to be?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: This was when the General Staff issued its first communique.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when was that, as you remember?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: This was in 1994, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You talked earlier about Adem Jashari. Can you tell the Court any involvement, any connection your family had to the Jashari family, Adem Jashari, as early on as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Until the case when the Jashari neighbourhood was surrounded and events occurring in 1992, we've had no family relation with Jashari Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. family. However, in this case with a war that was waged, we went to help Jashari family and we went to its neighbourhood. Also, many villages rendered help to the Jashari family, and my uncle went there to render his help and he was gravely injured during this event. And this has been my -- our connection with the Jashari group, our relation with the Jashari group -- or better to say, with the group of the Jashari family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear for the record, where is -- which town, which village, did this event, this battle you're talking about in 1992, take place? Where did that happen?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: This happened in Prekaz village near the town of Srbica, because Srbica includes also the neighbourhood of the Jashari family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, very briefly, can you explain to the Court who Adem Jashari was, what his role was in these events in the early 1990s.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I might say as much as I know. Adem Jashari -- I have known Adem Jashari even earlier on before I met him personally. And he took part in the demonstrations that occurred at the time -- and sorry, the next question -- can you repeat the next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was just asking what your -- who he was, the importance or significance of this man, who his role was, in your view.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Adem Jashari was the main protagonist and commander, a legendary commander, and general commander of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you first heard, you said, of the General Staff in a communique in 1994. Can you just tell us from your memory what was the content of that communique, what was the announcement that you remember?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I cannot remember the communique because there has been several communiques and I cannot remember exactly the content of the first communique.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you see other communiques from the General Staff after 1994 through -- let's say through 1998?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, there have been several communiques, but maybe I've not seen them all. But there's been lots of communiques that I have seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again an overly simple question, but what was the -- why was the General Staff issuing these communiques? What was the purpose?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I don't know because I haven't been a member of the General Staff. I wasn't honoured to have that post and that duty. I haven't been a member of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But you do recall reading these communiques when they were issued?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Sometimes I have seen those communiques, but I cannot recall their content.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, when you joined -- tell me what happened to you on January 30th, 1997. What did you do that day? You've already spoken about that was when you joined the Kosovo Liberation Army, but what happened on that day of your life?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: On January 30th, 1997, I went out publicly, I joined the group of Adem Jashari because this was an armed group and I joined the group of Prekaz, the group of Adem Jashari, the legendary commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, now at that point who was your direct superior?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: It was Adem Jashari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was the procedure when you joined? What did you have to do? Did you have to say anything, sign anything? What was the procedure?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: There has been no procedure at all because even earlier I've been a member of Adem Jashari. However, the reason why I joined the group in 1997, it was the arrest of my uncle's son. That's why I came out publicly and joined Adem Jashari group with arms. At the same time, I've kept contact with Adem Jashari and his group. However, there hasn't been any special statement or something else to sign because I've known him earlier and we have cooperated even earlier with Adem Jashari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: For others joining the KLA at this period, was there any oath that soldiers were required to take?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, later there has been an oath, and I saw -- and the rule was to take the oath in front of the flag, that they would not break the international law and they will obey the military orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you say you came out publicly. Once you publicly identified yourself with Jashari and joined in January 1997, what did that mean for you? What effect, what changes, did that cause in your life, where you lived?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: We started to get organised in a better way because our movement was limited. The oppression of the Milosevic regime was very high. They were evicting people, they were arresting people. And they were maltreating the population and the civilians. And so it changed my life a bit because I got the uniform of the KLA and we had a pure organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, where were you stationed?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: We were stationed in Prekaz in Adem Jashari. However, with -- as I came out publicly, myself, I stayed in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And why was that? Did anybody -- was there any reason why you were stationed in your village, your home town?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: The reason was simple, because I had many friends around me, some people who were armed, and the reason that it was not reasonable to stay in Prekaz any longer because I had my circle and I was trying to have people who were credible and people whom I trusted, in order because we wanted to expand the war and to expand it in several circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you explain what you mean by you wanted to expand the war in several circles.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: This is simple because -- not because I wand to expand, but my stance was that I stay at my home in the place where I was born and where I knew people even earlier. And those people were informed about our activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did you have any command responsibility at this point? Was there anybody who was under -- who you could issue orders to?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: No. At first, no, because Adem Jashari was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, during this time was Adem Jashari in contact with the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes. It is normal that Adem Jashari had contacts -- contact with the General Staff, and he had contacts that I was not aware of because I was not at the level that I would know about his activity and the General Staff. But it is known that he had contacts not only with the General Staff but also with other countries, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And why would he have contact with the General Staff, what was the nature -- what would the General Staff tell him to do or what was the -- what was the reason for these contacts?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I hope it is a question for the members of the General Staff and not for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you what you know, if you can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would make an observation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The witness indicated that he was unaware what communication if any was occurring between Adem Jashari and the General Staff, because that was not his position in a previous question just asked by Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that will clarified in the next answer. You're quite right so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So you can answer the question, General. You've explained the position you've held, but can you tell us from your knowledge, from your involvement in this group, what was the nature of the contact Adem Jashari had with the General Staff? What was the purpose of these contacts?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: As I said before, the purpose -- I don't know what the purpose was because I was not present there. However, our duty - and when I say "duty" as being only contacts with Adem and not contacts with the General Staff and the legendary commander Adem Jashari, because he was a commander and had contacts with the general staff and continuous contacts with the staff. I cannot elaborate more on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, Adem Jashari was your direct commander. What, if you can tell us, were the parameters of his area of responsibility or his zone of responsibility at this time?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Adem Jashari was based in Prekaz at his home; however, he had acted in other areas which I don't know. I don't know where were the areas he acted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, how many soldiers approximately were under his command at this time?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: What time you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The time immediately after you joined and became subordinated to him. So we're talking, about let's say February 1998 -- 1997, sorry.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: This was specific in our organisation because if I had known some people, then I cannot know some other people who were soldiers of Adem Jashari. I was -- it was impossible to know every one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not asking if you knew everyone. What I'm asking you is -- let's put it this way: Through 1997 when you were formally subordinated to Adem Jashari, what was your conception or impression of how large a force you were part of?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: As far as I know, I've known some people, probably 10 to 15 members. However, the impression has been different because they were organised people. At that time, I have not known more than the people I've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, I'm not asking who you personally know, but how many people you believe were, like you, similarly under the command of Adem Jashari, let's talk about through 1997.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I'm saying it again because I don't know how many people were under Adem Jashari's command. I can say the number that I've seen with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And was there any reason, any strategic reason, why members did not know each other at this time or were not all known to each other?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: This was a strategy that even any of us was imprisoned then he was not allowed to know the other person. I think this was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, again let's talk about this early period after you've formally joined and you're under Adem Jashari's command. What was the goal, what was the plan for your area, for the area you were working -- operating in?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: The goal was that if the Serbian forces were continuing to maltreat and imprison people, then we would go to help those people and those families.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, how long were you under the command of Adem Jashari?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Until he heroically fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you tell us exactly when that was?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Fighting occurred on the 5th, 6th, and the 7th of March.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just very briefly describe what occurred on those dates.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: At that time, some parts of the Drenica regiment were attacked; however, the main forces were dislocated in the village of Prekaz. And when Prekaz was surrounded heavy fighting took place there. However, on the 5th of March a group of tanks were placed in Jasanica, attacked the nearby villages, the village where I was born, and then later they managed to reach the village of Turiqevc and also other nearby villages, at the time fighting that occurred in Prekaz and Laus Pelas [phoen] and the suburbs. So during that fighting Commander Adem Jashari heroically fell, along with some members of his family and many other civilians who were in the neighbourhood. At that time my position at the time in my village, and when I start to help them they were confronting the Serbian forces who came from Jasanica at the factory and those forces were dislodged at the factory. And I think before coming to the 5th of March there had been a buildup of the Serbian forces in Jasanica in the mushroom factory, but there has been also informants and buildups of Serbian forces, forces with tanks and other ammunition at the factory, and the attack was combined at the same time. The first, Prekaz was attacked and at 6.00 in the morning the force was starting to attacked, coming from municipality of Klina, and precisely, from the village of Jasanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You referred at the beginning of your answer to the Drenica regiment. What was that?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I do not understand you. Drenica is where it's based on the map. I do not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said some parts of the Drenica regiment was attacked. I'm asking you to explain if you can where was the Drenica regiment, what Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. does that refer to, which regiment was that and what is its area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I said that -- even earlier that Prekaz was attacked along with the nearby villages. So Prekaz was attacked. Mainly the goal was to attack Adem Jashari, the legendary commander. The nearby villages were also attacked, and I said at the same time nearby villages around Junik and Drenica, or Belince, Jasarev, Turiqevc, Vunik [phoen], this has been the period when these events happened on the 5th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show you now, Witness, a map. This is from P1, map number 5. Now, can you just show me -- I don't think it's marked on here approximately where your home town Acareva where you described you were born, you lived, and where you were based.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: As from what I see, this is not a complete map, it doesn't mark all the places. If you can zoom it in, please. The part where Klina is, it doesn't show any of the villages, Orahovac. And even the existing ones are not easy to distinguish.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you just show us approximately where your town was. I'll try to find you a better one; this one is difficult for you. Let me give you --

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Just a second, sir. I want to explain something. You can see Klina town here, and the road Klina-Skenderaj-Srbica. I don't see Skenderaj here in this map, actually. I cannot see it here. There is no Skenderaj town in this map. I can of course explain to you the roads from Klina. In the middle of this road -- my village is situated in the middle of this road. It's called Turiqevc, from Turiqevc. No, from my village, Turiqevc is in the middle. From Turiqevc to my village it's 5 kilometres and a half. And this off-side road, Klina-Skenderaj road in the middle of Klina and Skenderaj is Acareva, my native village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, we'll do that again. I'll get a better map with more markings on it.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: That would be a good idea as I said, because this is an incomplete map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've described events after 5th of March, 1998. Tell me, what was the effect on the KLA and the numbers of volunteers for the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: It had a great impact because the heroic fall of the legendary commander and part of his family had a very large impact on the domestic opinion in Kosovo and outside Kosovo, because there were many compatriots living outside Kosovo. Many of them expressed their wish to join the Kosovo Liberation Army after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you've said many compatriots living outside Kosovo expressed their wish to join. What did they do? Did they in fact join?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: The Kosovo Liberation Army developed in stages. Up to 5th of March for many people it was not known. But after the heroic fall of Adem Jashari, it became -- it Kosovo Liberation Army drew the attention of many compatriots who wanted to join it or subscribe to it. And the number rose greatly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After March 1998, what was your position, what was your next command position?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: At this period, I -- as I said, I was a soldier of Adem Jashari. With my return to my native village we set up together with some other friends, we set up the Shkoza unit. There were other units in various places.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Which were these other units in various places? Can you tell us the ones you remember and where they were.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: As far as I remember, and I do remember well, there was the Shkoza 1 and 2 units that communicated with me; there was Sandokan in the other place; there were other points like Alpha 1, Alpha 2, led Muje Krasniqi; and some other points or units with different numbers. But each of them, after the fall of the legendary commander, they became independent of each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, who had overall command responsibility for the different units or points which you've discussed after Adem Jashari's -- the attack on his compound?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: There was no commander as yet. They still were existing as individual units. But we were seeking to organise ourselves, but we still remained, as I said, separate because his death was -- inflicted a heavy blow to the Kosovo Liberation Army. So we're still without a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in other regions you've spoken about Adem Jashari and his contacts with the General Staff. What other -- what was -- if you can tell us, what was the plan in other regions in Kosovo at this time? Not the immediate region which Adem Jashari has commanded, but in other regions as well.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I know nothing about other regions because, as I said, I was -- I didn't have any high-ranking positions, so I didn't have information about other places. But that organisation did exist, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm not speaking about your personal knowledge of detailed operations in other regions. What I'm trying to get at is that the KLA growth you've described and the KLA process, this acceleration after Adem Jashari's death, was that confined to just the Drenica region?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: The Drenica zone was a specific one because that was as a stronghold I would say of the Kosovo Liberation Army became public since 1992, and it had a very -- better organisation. The number of soldiers was greater compared to other regions. People often came to Drenica because they didn't find a better organisation in their own respective places.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you name for us some of the other regions, some of the other zones, which you've described as being less well-organised, less advanced.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: In the period I'm talking about, I mean 1998, after the fall of Adem, legendary commander Adem Jashari, that is what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I don't know how well-organised the other regions were, but I can speak about the organisation of my zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just what were the names of the other regions?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: At this time the other zones were not well-organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: These other zones which were not well-organised, can you tell me what the names of some of those zones were?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: After 5, 6, 7 March, it is a time of re-organisation, mobilisation, of the army. Up to -- this went on for some months, a time when other regions began to be organised. But how well organised they were, I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Through 1998, as these other regions are becoming organised - I'm not asking you how well-organised they were at this point - I'm just asking you to name what those other regions were. If you can tell me perhaps which other regions bordered the Drenica region.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: 1998 is a long period, but this was the time when other zones began to be organised as in Drenica. The Drenica zone I explained to you was more organised. But the bordering zones, Pastrik and Dukagjini and Shales were other zones. But Drenica is in the middle of Kosovo and maybe we border some part of Llap zone as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You talked about -- you started explaining this was a year, 1998, when the organisation developed, when it was it was re-organised and that recruits were coming in, it was growing. You also talked about points or units. What did these points or units evolve into? Did the terminology change at all?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, of course they did. Because, as I said, there were different units operating in the Drenica operational zone. And when something happened, the other units would ask for succour the other units [as interpreted]. So often we went to the rescue of one another. At this period, that is up to the end of May 1998, these were the units operating in that area. At the end of May, it was deemed appropriate to join. And after the fall of a legendary commander, as I said, we didn't as yet have a commander after his death. So the need arose for us to unite and for someone to resume responsibility and for the transformation of these units at a later phase into brigades. And then I was one who resumed the responsibility at the end of May 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And at the end of May 1998 when you resumed this responsibility, what was your title at that point?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: When the units met or the points, as we called them, operating in the Drenica area, when we united, the responsible persons of all these units in the presence of a member of the General Staff, we discussed who is going to take on the main burden for the organisation of the warfare in Drenica. So after that, this meeting in the presence of a member from the General Staff, they proposed me to become a zone commander. The request was sent to the General Staff, and the General Staff approved the request presented to them for me to become the commander of the 1st Operational Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I know this was some time ago, but can you give me your best recollection of when this meeting took place and when you were appointed commander of the 1st Operational Zone?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: The meeting was held at the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Which representative of the General Staff was present?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: The representative was a general inspector Rexhep Selimi, and he took in the opinions of all the responsible persons of the units for me to become the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just tell me now: Who, to your recollection, were members of the General Staff during 1998? I don't need you to break it down by month or anything like that, but who was a member during 1998 and what their titles or functions were.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I knew some of the members. I cannot tell you the exact number of the General Staff. I knew some of them who introduced themselves as such - Hashim Thaqi, Rexhep Selimi, Imres Kukrec [phoen], Sekurba Shoto [phoen] - with who I've had contacts during this period. There were, however, other members who I didn't know at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And during this period, talking about now from May 1998 through the end of 1998, where was the General Staff physically located? Where did they meet, the members of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: The members of the General Staff -- this is a good question if you ask me about them. If you ask me about myself, I was in Likovc. Because the members of the General Staff used to move to be on the run. Often they held meetings where there was a need arose for such meetings. There was not a place for such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand. And can you tell me some of the places these meetings would have been held in 1998, if you remember when meetings were held at different places.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I'm telling you, when some of them met in Drenica operational zone, I can tell you; but when they held meetings in other places, I cannot tell you because I was not present so I don't know. They know where they held the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How often were meetings held in the Drenica zone?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: The meetings were frequent I had with the brigade commanders. We had consultations first with the commanders of the points about how we were going to organise and form brigades. Sometimes these meetings were daily meetings, as often as we could when we were not fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you just give me, please -- give the court a time frame during these meetings you're talking about, these frequent meetings.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: After I was appointed zone commander, as I said, I had frequent meetings. I cannot tell you accurate figures. As I said, sometimes these meetings were held on a daily basis when we had time. It often happened that we didn't have meetings because of the fighting that went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand. And an additional -- in addition to meetings, did you communicate with members of the General Staff in any other way, by radio, telephone, courier, any other method?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: At a later phase, we communicated through telephone or through radio or direct contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: As a zone commander, was it important or necessary for you to know what was going on in the zones which bordered your zone?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: It was important, but not very important for me personally. For me personally, it was important how to keep -- to help the population in the zone and to fight the Serbian forces that attacked us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how would you find out when you were needed militarily in neighbouring zones? How was that information conveyed to you?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Often we tried to communicate through radio. Sometimes that has worked, sometimes not. There was a higher point through which we tried Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to communicate in Gasmaq -- that was the name of a place and through Buguri [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, between you as zone commander and the General Staff, was there any intermediate layer or level of command?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: No, there was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've talked about points and units, and I asked you about this before, but let me just complete this. Can you describe to the Trial Chamber exactly what a point was, whether it was described just a unit or soldiers or a place or -- exactly what a point meant militarily in 1998.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Until the time I became commander, they were called firing point.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Word for word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It consisted of a group of people operating in a certain area who had a certain code. With some people I used to serve in the Shkoza point, as I said earlier. Sometimes a number of the soldiers had a larger number; sometimes less soldiers. They might have the number of a platoon sometimes, sometimes less. The essence of the meaning is a group of soldiers who have a venue and they are deployed there and they have a code by which they are recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. So just to be very clear, it's a group of soldiers and it's also a geographic location?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, you might say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, can you tell me, please, as best you can - let's start in May 1998 onwards, May, June, July - how many men were under your command.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: The number kept increasing. When I am talking about May, the time I became zone commander, I had some, around -- after these points joined into brigades later, I had around 2 to 300 men, soldiers. But every day or every month, the number increased. And when we come at the end of 1998, I might speak of thousands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, I admit this is a rather broad question, but in your conception generally, what are your duties as commander? What are your most important duties as the zone commander?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: When I became zone commander, I started immediately to rally these points situated in various places and I started to form the brigades. Initially the number was not an adequate number in terms of brigades, but knowing that people were interested to join the army, I started to establish the brigades in this territory, that is Drenica. I set myself the task of forming the brigades and I started with Brigade 111, 112, 113, and 114.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just briefly, can you tell me who the commanders -- who you appointed to command those brigades.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes. After the units merged, those points, as I said, in each territory and area, I, as I said, started to form brigades. Initially it was 111. Jahir Djamllaku was the commander of that brigade. He operated in the area I used to work -- to fight, in Likovc. Brigade 112 was formed in the territory of point of Sandokan and covered an area of -- I might show it on the map if you had a map. It covered a territory from Runik [phoen], Skenderaj-Turiqevc, near Klina. Abedin Rexha was the commander. In Brigade 113 the commander was Muja Krasniqi. That brigade operated in the territory where I was -- had the staff of the operational zone. And there was part of special unit covering territory from Komorane, the asphalt road, Trenaz [phoen], Skenderaj, Klina, in the vicinity of Klina, up to Kiev. That was a territory covered by brigade 113, led my Muje Krasniqi. Brigade 114 has as the commander Fehmi Lladroci and it covered the territory of Drinovc [phoen], the asphalt road up to Skenderaj, the asphalt road up to Shipole [phoen] or in the vicinity of Shipole, and the line called -- near Cicavice, bordering the villages around Mitrovica up to Drinovc. That was the responsibility of Brigade 114, with commander Fehmi Lladroci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And which is the asphalt road you've been referring to? Which road is that?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: By asphalt road I mean Drenica-Skenderaj asphalt road. When I talk about asphalt road, I mean this. Skenderaj-Klina also is part of the line that divided the brigades. If you have a map, I could very well explain to you -- if you have a map of Drenica a little bit enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I will bring you an enlarged map after the break and you can show me these areas. Now, when you issued orders to these brigade commanders or to your point commanders, how were those issued? Were those issued in writing or orally or both? Can you describe how you would issue orders.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Often we gave orders in the decision when the commander was appointed. But because this was a time of re-organisation of the brigades, as I said, all -- it was the duty of all commanders to form brigades out of the units divided into platoons and companies and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand that, but I'm asking now generally. Did you issue orders in writing or just by speaking over the radio or in person to your commanders?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: It depends on the time we are talking about. When we are fighting -- there was fighting, it was impossible to send the order in writing. Often I gave it through the radio or orally when we met them, sometimes also in writing. All forms of communications were used by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is there any difference between a written order or a spoken order for the commander?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, what I mean is if you tell a commander, this is an order, speaking to him, or if you give him an order in writing, is there any difference in his duty to carry out that order? If you were speaking to a subordinate commander and giving him an order.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Every time I have given an oral order, I have made sure I send it also in a written form, when it was a matter of an operational order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when -- again though, when the commander receives that oral order, he is just as bound to carry out that order whether it is in writing or oral. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: We used to inform the commanders beforehand, but the decision is made in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you informed a subordinate commander, issued an order to him, what would you do to ensure that those orders were carried out?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: It depends if the commander was in a position to carry out the order, because often we couldn't communicate when there was fighting going on. I said that the operational zone had a specific character. We were always under attack, either on one side or the other side. So often the orders were not carried out, some of the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And are you saying that's because due to fighting conditions it was impossible for the order to be carried out? I just want to be clear that I understand your answer.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document now. This is U000-7684 behind tab 7 in the binder I'm giving you. Now, if you look at the photocopy of the original in your language - I apologise, the type is quite small - I'm interested in the one on the left side of the page, that's the one which is order number 3698, dated 31st of July, 1998, Likovac. I'll give you a moment to look at that document.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it. It's signed by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this is a ban on gathering of people in endangered places. It's to unit commanders. Now, we don't have much time before the break, but could you just tell us why you -- the order is fairly self-evident, but why did you issue this order at this time in July?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: It is very obvious. It was because in public places like schools or mosques or churches, they were -- all of them were identified as objects in military maps. And often the Serb forces attacked precisely these sites. This was a reason why I issued the order for the civilian population not to rally in these places for fear of some attacks, shelling, by the Serb forces. Because often the Serb forces attacked without discrimination and often where there were greatest rallies of civilians. That is the reason why I issued the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you look at point 4 on the order it states: "We refer to commanders of units and hold them responsible for the enforcement of this order." Is that what it says on the original in your language?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes. It is addressed to the unit commanders because when we gave the tasks to the brigade commanders to form the brigade, they continued to operate as units because they didn't have sufficient time to organise properly battalions and they still were referred to as units at this period of time. This was the reason why.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if a unit commander you found out had not acted on this order, had not enforced it, as demanded by the order, can you tell me what mechanisms were available to you to deal with that subordinate? What would you have done?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Everybody was interested to protect the population, and that was the crux of the order, actually, to protect the population in places where they were more endangered. So there was no need for them not to carry out that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand that. However, if you had found that if one of your subordinates had not carried out this order or another order like this, what would you have done to remedy that situation?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I don't know. I would say that opportunity didn't arise. None of them opposed the order, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I'm getting at is: When you had a subordinate what was the mechanism within your command at this time if somebody did not obey an order? Suppose a soldier deserted his post. What would happen to that soldier?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Until that time, nothing could happen to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What do you mean by "until that time"?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I mean, as I said, the essence of it. If a soldier thought that he didn't want to continue the service or had grounds not to do the service, there was nothing we could do because he came there on a voluntary basis and might leave if he wished. So because this is what he deemed appropriate to do, I mean to stay there in the army, to fight for as long as he wished. There was not any procedure in place to do anything if they wanted to withdraw from the army. They couldn't withstand the conditions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know if we're taking the break now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, if that's a convenient moment. We'll break now for -- until 10 minutes to 6.00 and then resume. --- Break taken at 5.29 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At some point there were formal military police units set up in the KLA. Let's talk now about in your zone.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: After my nomination as a commander, I had the responsibility to form the brigades, and after they were created, the military police and special units. The military police was created after my nomination -- well, I started to organise that a month or two months after I was nominated as a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was one of the duties of the military police to ensure that soldiers were behaving properly?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes. The military police had the responsibility to keep an eye on the discipline of the soldiers and also to take care of the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, from the beginning when you took command and while you were setting up these military police for these reasons, what actions could you take to discipline soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: In the beginning, we were in the process of consolidating the brigades. And the military police mostly dealt with -- well, even the military police was in the process of being organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand that. But during this period, in the beginning - I realise there was a lot going on, you were in combat - but if you had soldiers who misbehaved, who were drinking, who were creating other problems, what sanctions would be applied to them?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Very often we punished them by having them keep guard even outside their guard duties, outside their hours, or we gave them a notification -- a written notification not to behave like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And do you remember whether people -- soldiers were ever removed due to misbehaviour, stripped of their uniform and weapon and kicked out? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: No, I can't remember any such case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember -- let me just ask you if you remember talking about discipline in your interview with the Prosecutor, with the representatives of my office?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: No, I can't remember at this moment. If you can remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, do you remember in your first tape-recorded interview stating that one of the ways to enforce discipline was to take the weapons away from a soldier and his uniform and tell him that he can never be in the KLA again, and that this is most often what happened?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: It is possible. If they misused the gun or the weapon, the weapon was taken away from him. But if they improved, then they could get the weapon back. And we had very few weapons, so many soldiers did not have any weapons at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And if the soldier did not improve so that he should not be given his weapon back, then what would happen?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I have never run into such occasions. I have never seen such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I understand that you're very proud of your troops and that you think the soldiers in your unit were all good. But are you suggesting that there was never any need to discipline any of your soldiers ever during the summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I think that's how it was. I don't remember any cases when they needed to be disciplined. Or maybe there were some minor cases that I can't remember now, because it's been wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And let me just ask this to be very clear. Do you remember, ever, that a soldier from your unit was told that he could no longer be in the KLA, was removed from his unit?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in May 1998 -- well, sorry, let me go back to another topic and ask you another question. This is concerning your power as commander, your authority. If a soldier had committed a serious disciplinary offence, something dishonourable for a soldier of the KLA - for instance, assaulting a civilian - what would you have done to discipline that soldier? What was in your power to do?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Well, give him advice, these were the measures that were taken. Or when the soldiers are in uniform we gave him a warning or took his weapon away. There was nothing else we could do against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You could certainly take the weapon away, but couldn't you also kick this person out of their unit, remove them from duty?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: If they repeated the mistake, what they did, then they would be told to leave the unit. But it depended also on the commander of the unit, what their opinion was of this soldier and how this soldier behaved in other occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if a soldier had been told to leave the unit, how would that be seen in his home community, if he had to return, being kicked out?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I would make one observation that the level of speculation that is now being asked for this witness to engage in is a bit far afield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: From one view you're right, Mr. Guy-Smith; but there's another view that this is a question generally about the view in the community of which this witness was a member. And on that view, I think the question can be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: His Honour is stating that you may answer the question. If a young man joined the KLA and returned to his village because he had been kicked out, how would that be seen in the village? How would the community view that, based on your knowledge, living there, being there during this time, and being a commander in the Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Of course, of course, I was a commander. But I can't remember such cases happening ever, and I don't know how the community viewed them or that thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well -- and I'll move on. Do you think that would be viewed as a positive thing, as an achievement for a young man?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you're now going too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I don't know how it was viewed or communicated to the community, but if you have any concrete examples to put to me ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we're sort of a nil-all draw now, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, I was planning on taking your advice before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, let me show you a map. It's from Exhibit P1. Now, it may be -- yes, exactly, if you look to your left it may be clearer.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I can't see it very well on the monitor, so it's better if I look here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine. Now, do you see Likovac on that map?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you tell me where in relation to Likovac - I'm sorry, the town is not marked and named - but where the village you were born and grew up is.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: It's still -- it's only half a map, if I can say so. There are many villages missing from here. It would be on another part of the map, but it's not here. It's not very far from Likovc. It's only 4 kilometres from Likovc, probably only 4 kilometres and a half, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you indicate the direction from Likovac it would be 4 and a half kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: On the opposite side where you have here Baijice, my village is on the opposite side, not on the side where Baijice and the other villages are. It's on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, can you show me on this map - and it may not all be on here - looking at this map, what, if any, area was in your zone of command in May 1998?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: This map shows only a small part of that area. The parts that we can see in this map are those that are bordered by the asphalted road. It's the road to Pristina from Pec -- Peja to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, that Pec-Pristina road that you've identified, which border is that? Which side of that Pec-Pristina road is your zone of command?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: In the Drenica area where the Pristina-Peja road is included. So it -- Drenica is bordered -- Drenica border is -- this road marks that border.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So the Drenica region border is above the road, to the north of the road?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, as hesitant as I am to stand up and assist the Prosecution, I wonder if map 10, which after all is the General Staff's map of KLA zones as of January 1998 -- 1999 -- 1998, may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It might save some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you for the suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Looking at the map you have, is that right that the Drenica zone is the zone directly above on this map the Pristina-Pec asphalt highway?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The Drenica area, as I said, is bordered by this area, Pec-Pristina, the road. And the area where Belikovce [phoen] where the 113 Brigade operated. That was my operational area, including Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, on the map that you've got before you on the Pristina-Pec road, how much of that was within the responsibility, was the zone of the 113th Brigade? In other words, is it the entire road or part of it? You said including Lapusnik, but how far in either direction from Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: The 113th Brigade commanded by Muje Krasniqi operated from the village of Gllareve up to the Lapusnik gorge, up to Komorane. But the responsibility areas were divided by this asphalted road, and they were up to Likovc, Drenica and the asphalted road of Skenderaj, which is not here in the direction of Klina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if I could, I will follow my friend's suggestion and show you another map. This is map 10 from P1.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You see how the different KLA operational subzones are marked on this map?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, I can see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Looking at the Drenica zone, is that -- the area mapped out as the Drenica zone, is that roughly accurate, a map on this scale, from May through July 1998?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, more or less it's clear here, but there are many villages that are not marked here. But more or less, this is the zone, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the other zones on the map, are those also -- for a map of this scale, I know it doesn't have every village marked, the Pastrik zones, is that accurate map of the zones?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I don't know about the other zones, I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. The map's accurate, is it not, as you said earlier? The Pastrik zone was the zone bordering the Drenica zone, immediately below, south of the Drenica zone?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the units of the 113 Brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can take the map away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- which operated in the zone bordering the Pristina-Pec highway on either side of Lapusnik, what were the names of the points or units which made up that zone or which made up that brigade?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Starting with Alpha, which was -- which existed before the brigade was formed, Alpha, Alphane [phoen], Pellumbi, and Guri, they were stationed in this area. As far as I can remember, there was also Zogu. But these were also the ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear, these units became the 113th Brigade after you had established the brigades?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes. These units and other units that operated in the internal part of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Speaking of your zone. Now, which units in May, June, July operated on the other side of the Pristina-Pec highway, which was the zone boundary, on the other side matching the 113th Brigade and the units you've told us about?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I mentioned it earlier, Guri, Pellumbi, and Alpha. They were close to the asphalted line and they were under the responsibility of the 113th Brigade. But there was other units such as Shkoza and Mali and other units that operated in the internal area of the zone. But if you want to know which ones operated closer to the road, these are the ones that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And on the other side of the road, which units operated?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: This was a time of organisation and re-organisation. And when I was with these units on the other side there were no formations. There were some units, Celiku -- some units named Celiku, which at that time started becoming organised just like the units in my area. But at that time they were still working independent of each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The Celiku units were being organised at the same time as you were organising the units on your side of the Pristina-Pec highway border. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Exact -- I don't know exactly what kind of organisation were the Celiku units undergoing at that period. I explained to you the way my units were organised into a big brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, on the 9th of May, 1998 - you probably remember that date - what was going on with the 113th Brigade, the Pellumbi units, starting then, in their zone?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: At that time, the Serbian forces started entering the villages from Komorane and the Lapusnik gorge, and other villages around like Krekova [phoen] and other villages. When they started going into these villages we started re-organising and we started participating in fighting in the Lapusnik gorge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a famous battle, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, we fought as hard as we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Not just that you fought as hard as you could, but -- well, do you remember we met very briefly yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you remember -- we didn't discuss it, but I asked you if you remembered giving an interview. Zeri I think is the name of the --

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We met up yesterday, yes, with you. And you mentioned the Zeri interview and I have it in front of me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I gave you a copy of that interview in your language, didn't I? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, and I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Does that article -- you spoke about in that interview the Lapusnik gorge battle of May 1998. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, I mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like you, if you can, to explain to the Court, similarly as you did in that interview, in your own words, how -- the significance of this battle was for the KLA, why it was important that the Lapusnik gorge battle be won.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, that is clear. I explained it in the interview. I don't know how clear it is for you, but I can explain it to you now again, that the Lapusnik gorge was a very -- a point of interest for us - I'm speaking about the operational zone of Drenica. We were interested in that because we did not want the Serb forces to enter there with their tanks and other vehicles as they had done before. Our strategy for the area was to have a free corridor and to be able to have this corridor for transporting weapons for the KLA. I said that in the interview, and I'm saying it again, I tried to protect -- to defend this area with all my units. We fought to protect this Lapusnik gorge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you said that the road would have been used by the KLA then to transport -- to bring weapons in or things like that. Did the Serbs use this road for any purpose before the May 9th battle? What did the -- what did the Serb forces use this road for?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: In order to get into the villages with which -- which bordered the Drenica operational area, because often the Serb forces entered these villages. I -- my area of responsibility -- in my area of responsibility, the Serbs tried to infiltrate -- to get into the areas where there was civil population. They know what their purpose was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How long did this battle last, starting on May 9th?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I don't know. One day, two, until the gorge fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you say "the gorge fell," what exactly do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Until the Serb forces entered my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, let me go through this step by step with you. The battle is on May 9th. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: On your side, your zone of responsibility, the units fighting are the 113th Brigade under your command?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes. It was not a consolidated brigade yet; it was not properly formed. It was under the process of organisation. But these were units that were -- that operated in my operational area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. The units which would eventually become the 113th?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: On the other side of the Lapusnik gorge, on the other side of the highway, you said there were the Celiku units.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, the Celiku units. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: These Celiku units, how did they participate in the May 9th battle for the gorge?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: At that time, there were many units, maybe some units named Celiku. I don't know many exactly there were. And I knew Celiku Number 1, but as I said there were several Celiku units and they were operating independent of each other. And I don't know the areas where they operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where was Celiku 1 located on May 9th? Where was that point?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where they were situated. I did not operate in their area, I was in my area of responsibility. But I knew that Celiku Number 1 existed. But would think it could be approximately in Klecka. I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The units on the other side of the road, the Celiku units, were also in combat on May 9th. Is that right? Part of this battle.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was the number of the brigade that these Celiku units were eventually formed into?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: At that time you could not speak about a brigade, but they were only units, small groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand that. When they became a brigade, what was the brigade number, the name of that brigade, the number of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: The Celiku unit, some of them went into the 122nd Brigade, the others 121st Brigade. Maybe in other brigades, but I'm not clear about that, where they joined and how they were divided into brigades. I know that there were Celiku units in the 122nd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the 121st?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Some of them were also in the 121st Brigade, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, do you remember in that article stating to the interviewer --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this has ridden long enough, with the greater of respect. My friend has previously, before the break referred to a tape-recorded interview, and he now seeks to refer to an interview with a newspaper. Your Honour, of course this is not a memory test. The witness has been provided with these documents. He has used them as a memory-refreshing document prior to giving evidence today. In my respectful submission, the witness should be asked what he remembers, rather than what he said in a newspaper. Your Honour, it's as basic as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The point is well made, Mr. Nicholls. You seemed about to go to say, Remember something you said in an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
