utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I was going to ask him if he remembered a topic and ask if he wanted to -- I was going to try to direct him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you can direct him to a particular topic without going to past interviews, can you not? And then you can seek whatever information you think is relevant about that topic, again without going to past interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you know Fatmir Limaj?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes, I know him quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When did you first meet him in person?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I first met him in person in 1996, but I was not aware he was Fatmir Limaj, and I have explained this earlier. When he came back from the west, I met him and he seemed to me to be a public figure. And then they told me that he was Fatmir Limaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you say when you met him when he came back from the west, when is that? When did Fatmir Limaj come back from the West?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: This was after the heroic fall of the legendary commander. It was a period when many people came back from the west, and it was exactly the time when I met Fatmir Limaj as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Where did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Excuse me, I cannot remember exactly. It might be possible I met him in Likovc or Acareva, in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what was the context of the meeting? Why did you meet him at this time after he came back?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I met him with some other colleagues who also had come back from the west, and I just met him simply as Fatmir, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you met him, what name was he introduced to you by?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: First there was -- no name was introduced to me. Then afterwards or at the time -- first it was not clear to me whether he was introduced to me as Fatmir or Celik, but it was the time when I knew him as Celiku. I'm not sure and it's might be possible that he was introduced to me as the uncle, "Daja," if I remember it quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you've just stated that he was introduced to you as Fatmir or Celiku after March 1998.

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: I said I cannot remember quite well because I've met him even later as Celiku, but I cannot remember quite well how he was introduced to me during the period I met him. Later on I came to know him as Celiku, but for the period we met, it is not clear whether he was introduced to me as Daja because it was a short -- it was a very short time. We just met and we shake hands with each other and we just greeted each other. And there was the -- there was no other conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When -- well, you've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I point out, Mr. Nicholls, that the date of the meeting appears in the transcript as March 1998. I thought the oral evidence was March 1996. Is the transcript in error or my recollection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think it's March 1998. We can ask the witness to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Witness, you met Fatmir Limaj you said after the death of Adem Jashari. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think I understand, Your Honour, he spoke about two occasions that he met Mr. Limaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, if you would be good enough to clarify --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, I'd like to clarify it once again. As I said, I met Fatmir Limaj in 1996, along with Rexhep Selimi along with two other friends, students. But I was not -- I did not know at the time he was Fatmir Limaj. After I met him the second time as a soldier of the KLA, I met him after March and after the heroic fall -- death of commander Adem Jashari. And I cannot then remember exactly when that was, maybe in April. I don't know whether I explained it clearly to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think I will intervene directly, Mr. Nicholls. When you first met the person Fatmir Limaj, you said you -- this was in 1996 and you did not then know him as Fatmir Limaj. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. When I met him in 1996, I spoke with him but I was not -- I did not know who he was. But then in 1998 I recalled when I met him again then I came to realise that he was Fatmir Limaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Were you introduced to him by any name in 1996 when you first met?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, we were not introduced but we just met occasion -- we just ran into him. The son of my uncle talked to them and I was at Pristina hospital. At the time we did not sit down to drink something together, but I could just recall him by face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you meet Fatmir Limaj again in 1998, one of the names you know him as is Celiku. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The Celiku units in the battle of Lapusnik gorge on March -- in May 1998, where did they get their name "Celiku" from? Where were they named after?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: The units from Komorane, I don't know because it is not the area of my responsibility. However, it has been repeated and said very often. I don't know where they took the name from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the Celiku units in the battle for the Lapusnik gorge on May 1998?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: It is clear that I explained it earlier where the units acted. The units that existed did not act on the other side, they did not have a commander. They were independent units and were acting independently. When the need be, the unit would go and tell the other unit. Or when our unit sought help from the other one. So when this was on my side and this also -- how it was the other side acted. This was for the simple reason - if I am allowed to continue - the units, as I said, were not uniform, did not have a commander. Each of those units had a command at one point until - I'm just saying this from my experience - until a decision was taken to be a commander of one zone or a commander of one brigade and to form that brigade. So at the time, the units acted as independent ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now I'm going to go back to the interview you gave to the magazine -- to the publication Zeri in 2000. Were you truthful in the statements you made when you spoke and conducted that interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's a proper question, but your moment may come very shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the question is lost, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because I have not received Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the question yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You stated you were truthful when you spoke to the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor. You stated you were truthful when you spoke to the Defence. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SYLEJMAN SELIMI
utterances.text: Yes. I've said that I've told the truth, and I have in fact told the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, you asked a question to which there is not yet an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you going to put that question again or are you leaving it alone?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm leaving it alone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I ask that the witness be excused from the court for a moment. I have an application to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. General, if you would be kind enough to wait outside the court, there is an application of some type to be made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. However, if you need, I can explain it, even what happened after the interview or I can explain it to you right now before leaving the hall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you better wait outside. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The witness -- I've now asked him several questions which are exactly the same as questions he was asked either in the interview conducted by Defence counsel or the interview conducted by the Office of the Prosecutor. He's given different answers. I think it's apparent in the courtroom today -- than he gave in those interviews. I think it's apparent from his demeanour and from his evasion of some questions that he does not want to answer questions I put to him and is being evasive. Mr. Khan made the point at the beginning of this session that the witness said that he did not want to be a witness for the Prosecution, that he refused -- that he would like to be a witness for the Defence. So at this time I think I've reached a point where I must ask for the Court's permission to treat him as an adverse or a hostile witness. He's certainly adverse under the rules which I would practice under and Mr. Guy-Smith does in the United States. He's aligned with the other party. He's openly aligned himself with the opposing party. He is also hostile in the sense that he is resisting as much as he can asking questions. Now, I did not proof this witness, I did not discuss his testimony with him beforehand. But in his interviews with the Prosecution - his taped interviews which we have on videotape as well as on -- it's not just an audio recording, it's a video recording - he was very plain and open about certain issues and he made statements which are completely different from the ones he's making today. So he has become hostile. He stated at the end of that interview that no pressure had been put on him; that he was speaking of his own free will. And he stated in court today here that he was truthful in those previous interviews, not just to our office but to the Defence. We have notes of the Defence interviews where he gave answers different to these. So I request that at this point the Court -- the Trial Chamber give me permission to treat him as a hostile witness, use leading questions, and to put his previous statements to him. I think it's important for the Court to get an accurate depiction of the probative evidence that this witness has to offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be important, Mr. Nicholls, if the Chamber is to evaluate your application for there to be some clear indication of materially different answers on this occasion from the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can provide that, Your Honour. There are several. In the interview --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you on your feet, Mr. Topolski?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No, I'm preparing to be, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can provide that to Your Honour. In the interview, the witness states that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Which interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm speaking of the transcripted interview of the Office of the Prosecutor of the -- sorry, I'll give you the date. 19 November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 2003, Your Honour. Now, it's at tab 19, Your Honours, of your binder. Now, in that interview the witness stated that he was introduced to Fatmir Limaj, and I'm looking at page 36. The witness was asked a question: "Q. Did you know Fatmir Limaj was called Celiku?" "A. Not in the beginning. The first time I met him, I didn't know his name. Okay." He then states: "When I knew him, I knew him as Celiku. Afterwards, I learned his name as well." And at the bottom of the page, Your Honours, the witness goes on to say that he had met Fatmir Limaj earlier but didn't know his name. On page 37 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is the difficulty about that evidence in contrast to the evidence we have had today?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, because the evidence today -- the witness has stated that he didn't remember whether he was introduced in 1998 as Fatmir Limaj or as Celiku or as Daja, whereas throughout the interview the Prosecutor's interview of 2003 the witness only uses the names Celiku and Fatmir Limaj. Additionally, he says on page 37 of the English: "After a month or two," -- and it's clear now from the interview the period we're talking about is 1998 -- "I knew his name as Fatmir, but at the beginning it was the Celiku unit's commander." That's how he states he knew Fatmir Limaj in May 1998. Now he stated he's not sure about the name, which was first, and also stated that there was no commander of the Celiku units, that they acted sort of independently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, you've moved points there. But on the question of names it was in a very confused state when the evidence was first given, and I think that was the point at which I intervened. And as I understood his evidence on my intervention, it was that he didn't know his name at all in 1996 when they first met; that in May 1998, when they met for the second time, he knew him as Celiku; and later he learned his name to be Fatmir Limaj. That is not, it seems to me, materially different from what is at page 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. Well, what -- I may have -- I don't have it in front of me, but I thought -- my recollection was he was not clear on which name he knew first in 1998. I may be in error on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That happened in the first passage of evidence, page 46, line 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Additionally, though, and as important, the witness has stated now that he doesn't know or remember who commanded the Celiku units and tried to say that these units were working independent of each other and he's not sure. Whereas on page 37 of the interview it's quite clear that he knew Fatmir Limaj as the Celiku unit's commander. That is exactly in line with what the witness says in his prior statement in 2000 in the interview with the magazine article. That's at tab 18 of the binder. On page 13 of that interview in the third paragraph from the bottom, amongst other things the witness states: "The units of the future 121st Brigade led by their commander, Celiku, Fatmir Limaj, were operating on the other side." This portion of the article begins on the prior page, page 12, is concerned only with the battle in Lapusnik on May 9th. The other point of contradiction - it may take me a moment to find it, Your Honour - is that in the interview at page 36 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was that tab 19 again?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Page -- sorry, 35, 36. The witness is asked: "Do you have an explanation of where the Celiku units got their name from?" At the bottom of page 35. He states first he's not sure. Then on the top of page 36: "It was -- maybe because of his character, the way the units fought." The investigator asks him: "Fatmir's?" "A. Yeah." Then there's the discussion in the interview of how he learned Fatmir Limaj was called Celiku. So the witness is now contradicting these points, that Celiku -- Fatmir Limaj was commander of the Celiku units; at the battle of Lapusnik, that they fought on the other side of the road from his units under Celiku's command at that time in early May 1998, and that in fact these units were named after their commander because of his character and his competence. So these are material departures from his interview which he has stated was truthful. As well as from the Zeri interview where he states very bluntly that the units of the future 121st Brigade, which he stated were the Celiku units, were led by their commander, Celiku, Fatmir Limaj, on May 9th. And I did not expect these answers from him based on his interview, based on watching his demeanour during the interview on videotape. I wasn't present at the interview with the Office of the Prosecutor. As well as the notes I've been provided of the Defence interview, which the witness attend on the 25th of -- excuse me, on the 11th of October, 2004. Now, I don't have a tape of that interview, but my notes -- the notes of the investigator who was present state that the Defence asked the witness if he knew the pseudonym --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm providing is I think what Your Honour asked me for is examples of material differences and what the witness is stating here in court now and what he's stated earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Khan's point is that this last is based on something that is not presently in a recorded form and able to be placed before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, it's in a recorded form -- they have a record, a tape-record, of it. And what I have is a record of the notes of the investigator who was present at the interview. This is the only interview conducted by the Defence of a witness in which the witness stated that a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor could be present and was -- he had no objection to that and allowed the investigator to be present and take notes. So it is in a recorded form that I can put before the Court. And the difference here, Your Honour, is something a bit different from the earlier examples I've mentioned because the Defence asked the witness if he knew the pseudonym of Fatmir Limaj, and he replied that he "always knew him as Celiku, always." That's markedly different and it's an important point from what he stated the first time in any interview - either with us, the Defence, or the press - about the nickname. This Daja, uncle, has never come up before. And in the Defence interview he affirms that the only nickname he knew Fatmir Limaj as is Celiku. This is a recorded form I can put before the Court. And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I suspect that you will need to do that tomorrow, Mr. Nicholls, given the hour. As you know, we cannot go beyond 7.00 or there are difficulties for the accused in their return to custody. So we will need to break at this point, and I would invite you to give consideration to the manner in which you will found that last submission of yours on material to put before us. Now, I've been conscious, Mr. Khan, that I've not ignored you but thought that there was a matter that ought to be dealt with directly. Is there something that you want to put at this stage in addition to what I've been putting to Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm content to respond after my friend his completed his submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. I hope you don't think me too rude, but I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- dealing with one issue and trying to get it done in the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm most grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will need to adjourn now. The witness will need to be brought in now for a moment, and we will continue the submission when we resume tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: General, it is necessary because of our physical arrangements to finish at 7.00 in the evening, and we have reached that hour. The counsel are still putting submissions to the Chamber on a matter, and that will have to be continued tomorrow. When that matter is resolved, your evidence will continue. I'm sorry for this interruption, but I must ask now that you return tomorrow to continue your evidence. The resumption will be at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon. We will adjourn now for the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 18th day of January, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.
